\title{OrthoHPI 2.0: Predicting host--parasite protein--protein interactions
across multiple hosts at cell-type resolution}

\author[1,3]{Ida K.S. Meitil}
\author[2]{Juan Esteban Vargas Gomez}
\author[2]{Yesid Cuesta Astroz}
\author[1,3]{Alberto Santos}

\affil[2]{Escuela de Microbiolog\'ia, Universidad de Antioquia, Medell\'in,

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Parasitic infections cause a large global disease burden, yet the molecular
interactions between parasite and host remain poorly characterised for most
species. Knowing which parasite proteins interact with which host proteins can
reveal infection mechanisms and point to drug and vaccine targets.

We present OrthoHPI 2.0, which predicts host--parasite protein--protein
interactions (PPIs) by orthology transfer of intra-species interactions from
STRING. Only protein pairs that can physically interact are retained: host
proteins must be expressed in the tissues the parasite infects, and both
proteins must be in subcellular compartments where they can meet. Version 2.0
extends the resource from one host to four (human, pig, mouse, and rat) and
from 15 to 46 parasites. Predictions are now resolved to the cell-type level
using single-cell atlas data, and subcellular localization is predicted with
DeepLoc 2.1.

All predictions are available through an interactive web resource, where users
can browse the PPI network of a host--parasite pair, filter by confidence
score, tissue, cell type and localization, view AlphaFold models of interacting
pairs, and explore Gene Ontology enrichment of the interactors. Further pages
compare parasites of the same host and compare the hosts of multi-host
parasites.

OrthoHPI 2.0 generates testable hypotheses and enables comparison across
parasites sharing a host, or hosts of the same parasite, revealing common and
unique interaction strategies.
\end{abstract}

We have previously developed OrthoHPI, a tool that predicts host--parasite
PPIs by orthology transfer of intra-species interactions from the STRING
database~\cite{cuestaastroz2019analysis}. The method constrains transfer by
including only high-confidence intra-species interactions, using fine-grained
orthology assignment (EggNOG~\todo{ref} eukaryote groups), and constraining the
predictions to host proteins expressed in a tissue that the parasite infects
(TISSUES~\todo{ref}) and host and parasite proteins with a cellular
localization where they are physically able to interact. For cellular
localization, this version used the COMPARTMENTS database~\todo{ref} for host
proteins, and SignalP~\todo{ref}, TargetP~\todo{ref} and TMHMM~\todo{ref} to
predict the parasite protein localization.

\todo{How has OrthoHPI been used? Any nice results came out of people using
it?}

Here we present OrthoHPI 2.0, which extends the resource from one host to four
(human, pig, mouse, and rat), and from 15 to 46 parasites. We use DeepLoc
2.1~\cite{dum2024deeploc} for prediction of subcellular localization of both
the host and parasite proteins. We further extend the resource to include
cell-type level resolution for human, pig, and mouse, by utilizing single-cell
atlas data. Finally, we provide an interactive web resource that allows for
detailed investigation of individual host--parasite PPI networks as well as
comparisons across parasites and hosts at different score thresholds.

\section{Materials and methods}

% The stages below mirror docs/pipeline.md, which is the running description
% of what `python -m pipeline.main` actually does. Keep the two in step.

\subsection{Proteomes}
The hosts are the four species covered by the TISSUES database~\todo{ref}:
human, pig, mouse and rat. The parasites are the 46 endoparasites of these
hosts that have a proteome in STRING v12.0~\todo{ref}
(Table~\ref{tab:parasites}). Two parasites infect human, mouse and rat
(\textit{Hymenolepis diminuta} and \textit{Cryptosporidium muris}), two infect
human and pig (\textit{Trichinella spiralis} and \textit{Trichinella
pseudospiralis}), four infect mouse and rat (\textit{Angiostrongylus
cantonensis}, \textit{Angiostrongylus costaricensis}, \textit{Leishmania
braziliensis}, and \textit{Nippostrongylus brasiliensis}), and the remaining 38
infect only human. Each parasite is annotated with the tissues it occupies in
its host during its life cycle, with whether it is unicellular or
multicellular, and with whether it is intracellular or extracellular. A
parasite with an intracellular stage in the host is recorded as intracellular
even if another stage is extracellular (e.g.\ \textit{Plasmodium} spp.,
\textit{Trypanosoma cruzi}), since the intracellular stage has a wider reach.

\input{tables/parasites}

\subsection{Proteome filtering}
Interactions are predicted only between proteins that can physically meet. For
each host--parasite pair, the host proteome is narrowed to the proteins
expressed where the parasite is and localized where the parasite can reach,
and the parasite proteome to the proteins localized where it can reach the
host proteins.

A host protein is kept if TISSUES~\todo{ref} gives it an expression confidence
score of at least 1.0 in at least one of the tissues the parasite occupies.

Localization is predicted for every host and parasite protein with DeepLoc
2.1~\cite{dum2024deeploc}, Accurate model (ProtT5 embeddings). A protein is
assigned to a class when its class probability exceeds DeepLoc's own per-class
threshold for the Accurate model (Extracellular 0.617, Cell membrane 0.565,
Cytoplasm 0.476, Nucleus 0.501); a protein can belong to several classes.

For an extracellular parasite, host proteins are kept if they are predicted
extracellular or cell membrane. For an intracellular parasite, cytoplasm and
nucleus are added, since the parasite reaches the cytoplasm and nucleus. The
surface proteins are retained, because an intracellular parasite also has an
invasive extracellular stage.

On the parasite side, a unicellular parasite faces the host with its plasma
membrane, so its proteins are kept if predicted extracellular or cell
membrane. A multicellular parasite's cell membrane is buried inside the
organism and it reaches its host with secreted proteins alone, so only
proteins predicted extracellular are kept.

\subsection{Homology transfer}
Interactions are transferred from STRING's orthologous-group level network
(\texttt{COG.links.detailed}, v12.0), in which the intra-species interactions
of every STRING species are summarized between EggNOG 6.0~\todo{ref}
orthologous groups. Every eligible host and parasite protein is mapped to its
group at the eukaryote level (taxonomic level 2759). A host--parasite protein
pair is predicted to interact if their two groups are linked in STRING with an
experimental-evidence score or a database-evidence score of at least 0.7
(STRING scores divided by 1000). The OrthoHPI confidence score is the mean of
the two channel scores, so it ranges from 0.35 (one channel at 0.7, the other
at 0) to 1.0 (both channels at 1).

\subsection{Cell-type annotation}
For human, pig and mouse, host proteins are further annotated with the cell
types that express them in each tissue, from single-cell transcriptome atlases:
the Human Protein Atlas single-cell type data (\todo{ref}, version 23) for
human, the Pig Single Cell Transcriptome Atlas (\todo{ref}, release 2022-10-14)
for pig, and the Tabula Muris Senis~\todo{ref} for mouse. Rat has no comparable
atlas and is given tissue resolution only. Atlas tissues are mapped onto the
TISSUES tissue vocabulary used above. For mouse, only the 3-month-old animals
are used, from the droplet dataset, with the FACS dataset as a fallback for
tissues the droplet dataset lacks. So that all three hosts share one scale, pig
and mouse expression is computed the way the Human Protein Atlas computes it:
the raw counts of all cells of a (tissue, cell type) are pooled and scaled to
one million transcripts. A protein is annotated to a cell type when its
expression there exceeds 1 nTPM. Cell-type annotation is not used to filter
predictions, but as an extra annotation layer.

\subsection{Structural modelling of predicted interactions}
To test whether the predicted interactions can be modelled using
AlphaFold3~\todo{ref Abramson 2024}, we created a small benchmarking dataset.
Since the predicted interactions can reflect membership of the same complex,
where a model of the two proteins alone is not expected to show an interface,
we only included interactions transferred from direct binding, alongside a
human reference complex.

Human physical interactions were taken from BioGRID (release 5.0.262) and
IntAct (release of 10 January 2026). An interaction was considered direct if
BioGRID recorded it by two-hybrid, reconstituted complex, co-crystal structure,
far-western, protein-fragment complementation, protein--peptide or biochemical
activity assay, or if IntAct typed it as a direct interaction, an enzymatic
reaction, cleavage or covalent binding. Proteins were matched between the
databases and the orthologous groups by gene name. We considered predicted
interactions with a human host whose two orthologous groups contain a pair of
human proteins with direct evidence, and divided them by confidence score into
six bins (0.35--0.5, 0.5--0.6, 0.6--0.7, 0.7--0.8, 0.8--0.9, 0.9--1.0). Eight
interactions were drawn per bin, at most one per pair of orthologous groups,
from the parasites in turn, and excluding pairs longer than 1{,}500 residues in
total. This gave 48 interactions from 25 parasites.

The reference for each interaction was the human pair of its orthologous
groups with direct evidence, preferring pairs that include the predicted human
partner, then the pair with the most publications reporting direct binding.
For 27 interactions the reference shares the predicted human partner.
References were limited to 2{,}500 residues, since human proteins with direct
evidence are often longer than their parasite counterparts.

Each predicted and reference pair was submitted to the AlphaFold Server with
default settings (5--8 October 2026), giving five models per pair. For the
top-ranked model we report the interface predicted TM-score (ipTM) and the
ipSAE score~\todo{ref Dunbrack 2025}. ipSAE was computed from the predicted
aligned error matrix with a 10\,\AA{} cutoff, and is less sensitive than ipTM
to disordered regions outside the interface. An interface was considered found
at an ipSAE of at least 0.1.

To assess whether references might score higher because more evolutionary
information is available, we counted the rows of the paired multiple sequence
alignment built by the AlphaFold Server in which both chains have a homolog. A
row is counted as a homolog when at least 10\% of its aligned positions are
residues rather than gaps. The server's alignments are limited to 50{,}000
rows.

\subsection{The web resource}
All predictions are available in an interactive resource at
\url{https://orthohpi.streamlit.app}. For a chosen parasite and host, the
predicted network is shown as an interactive graph and as a downloadable
table, and can be filtered by confidence score, by tissue, by cell type, and by
the DeepLoc class of the host protein. The host and parasite proteins of the
network are tested for enrichment of Gene Ontology biological processes with
Fisher's exact test and Benjamini--Hochberg FDR, with the enriched terms shown
in their GO hierarchy. AlphaFold~\todo{ref} monomer structures of both
interactors are retrieved from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and
displayed for any selected interaction. Further pages compare the host
interactors shared between parasites, and for a parasite with several hosts,
the interactions shared between and specific to each host.

\section{Results}

\subsection{The predicted networks}
We predict 53{,}623 PPIs across 46 parasites and four hosts (36{,}515 in
human, 8{,}821 in mouse, 5{,}940 in rat and 2{,}347 in pig). The predictions of
every host--parasite pair are given in Table~\ref{tab:parasites}, split by the
localization of the host protein in Supplementary
Figure~\ref{fig:networks} and scored in Supplementary
Figure~\ref{fig:confidence}. Network size ranges from a single interaction
for the microsporidian \textit{Trachipleistophora hominis} to 3{,}509 for
\textit{Trypanosoma cruzi}.

Network size follows the way of life of the parasite (Supplementary
Figure~\ref{fig:funnel}; counts in Supplementary Table~S1). Two things set how
much of the host a parasite can reach: how many tissues it infects, and whether
it gets inside host cells. \textit{T.~cruzi} does both. It invades almost any
nucleated cell and replicates free in the cytoplasm of heart, gut and skeletal
muscle cells~\todo{cite}, so it meets many tissues and the host cytosol, and it
has the largest network. The \textit{Trichinella} species, whose larvae remodel
a skeletal muscle cell into a nurse cell, likewise have large networks
(3{,}050 for \textit{T.~britovi}).

Tissue breadth alone can separate close relatives. In rat,
\textit{Angiostrongylus costaricensis} lives in the intestine and meets 4{,}456
host proteins. \textit{A.~cantonensis}, whose larvae migrate through the brain
before the adults settle in the pulmonary arteries, meets 9{,}408. The two
contribute similar numbers of secreted and surface proteins (1{,}392 and
1{,}547), yet get 208 and 554 predicted interactions.

How the parasite touches the host matters as well. An extracellular parasite
reaches only the host's surface and secreted proteins, never its interior. The
route of contact differs even between helminth groups. Nematodes secrete
7--16\% of their proteome, against 4--8\% in trematodes and cestodes
(Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:deeploc_pools_parasite}), in line with the
central role of nematode excretory--secretory products in tissue invasion and
immune modulation~\todo{cite}. Flatworms meet the host mainly through the
tegument, a syncytial outer layer; its membrane proteins are not kept for
multicellular parasites (Discussion).

Conservation sets the ceiling, because an interaction can only be transferred
to a protein whose orthologous group carries one. Among the secreted and
surface proteins, 41--66\% are in such a group in nematodes, flatworms,
\textit{Plasmodium} and \textit{Leishmania}, against 17--39\% in the other
protozoa and the microsporidia. The lowest is \textit{T.~vaginalis} at 18\%
(791 of 4{,}443), whose genome is one of the largest among the protozoa and
expanded by lineage-specific gene families~\todo{cite Carlton et al.\ 2007}.
The same limit explains the smallest networks: the microsporidia are obligate
intracellular fungi with reduced genomes and fast-evolving
proteins~\todo{cite}. Conservation therefore works against the proteins that
matter most, since those most specific to a parasite, such as variant surface
antigens, are often the ones acting directly on the host. How far the
transferred links are structurally plausible is examined below.

\subsection{Shared host interactors across parasites}
To investigate which human parasites interact with the same human proteins, we
show in Figure~\ref{fig:similarity} the Jaccard similarity of the sets of human
proteins reached by each parasite. Where a parasite lives matters more than
what it is related to. The intracellular \textit{Trichinella} species are more
similar to the intracellular protozoa than to the other nematodes, and
\textit{T.~cruzi} is closer to \textit{P.~falciparum} (0.29) than to its
congener \textit{T.~brucei} (0.05). The two trypanosomes illustrate the point:
\textit{T.~brucei} lives free in blood and tissue fluids and escapes antibodies
by switching its variant surface glycoprotein coat~\todo{cite}, whereas
\textit{T.~cruzi} hides and replicates inside host cells. A parasite within a
host cell has access to the host cytoplasm, membrane traffic and nucleus,
whatever its phylogeny, while an extracellular parasite, from a blood-dwelling
trypanosome to an intestinal worm, meets the cell surface and the
extracellular matrix. Part of this split also follows from the method, since
the host localization filter differs between the niches
(Figure~\ref{fig:workflow}).

Within a niche, related parasites are more alike. Most clearly, the five
\textit{Trichinella} species reach nearly the same host proteins (Jaccard
similarity 0.65--0.81). They share the same life cycle, in which the larvae
invade skeletal muscle cells, and differ mainly in host range, geography and
whether the nurse cell is encapsulated~\todo{cite}, traits that are unlikely to
be visible at the level of conserved protein interactions.

% paper/figures/parasite_similarity.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/parasite_similarity}
  \caption{Jaccard similarity of the sets of human proteins reached by each
  pair of parasites. The strips along both axes show each parasite's taxonomic
  group and niche. The diagonal is left grey.}
  \label{fig:similarity}
\end{figure}

Next, we investigated which human orthologous groups the parasites share. Each
is the EggNOG orthologous group of a host protein, and can hold several
paralogues. Because extracellular parasites outnumber intracellular ones, a
single count over all 43 human parasites would favour the groups extracellular
parasites reach, so in Figure~\ref{fig:shared_ogs} we show the groups reached by
at least half of the parasites of each niche. Of the 909 groups reached by at
least two parasites, 13 meet this. Extracellular parasites can only reach host
proteins of the cell membrane or the extracellular space, so these are the only
groups the two niches can share, and six of them fall into two broad themes.

The first is the host cell surface and the extracellular matrix, the first
host structures any parasite meets: the laminins (37 parasites), the integrin
$\beta$ subunits (36), the amyloid precursor proteins (36) and dystroglycan
(31). Many of these are known pathogen targets. Laminin is bound by
\textit{T.~cruzi}, \textit{Leishmania} and \textit{Entamoeba} during adhesion
and invasion~\todo{cite}, and the hookworm neutrophil inhibitory factor blocks
the leukocyte integrin CD11b/CD18~\todo{cite Moyle et al.\ 1994}. Integrins are
entry receptors for bacteria such as \textit{Yersinia}~\todo{cite Isberg and
Leong 1990} and for adenoviruses~\todo{cite Wickham et al.\ 1993};
and dystroglycan is the receptor of \textit{Mycobacterium leprae} on Schwann
cells and of Lassa virus~\todo{cite Rambukkana et al.\ 1998; Cao et al.\ 1998}.
Among the groups just short of half of the intracellular parasites, heparan
sulfate proteoglycans anchor \textit{Plasmodium} sporozoites to
hepatocytes~\todo{cite Frevert et al.\ 1993}, NPC1 is the entry receptor of
Ebola virus~\todo{cite Carette et al.\ 2011; C\^ot\'e et al.\ 2011} and
neuropilin-1 a cofactor of SARS-CoV-2~\todo{cite Cantuti-Castelvetri et al.\
2020; Daly et al.\ 2020}.
That so many parasites converge on proteins that unrelated pathogens are known
to hijack suggests these are general points of entry into, and attachment to,
host tissue. The amyloid precursor protein is of particular interest for the
parasites that reach the brain, such as \textit{Toxoplasma gondii} and
\textit{A.~cantonensis}, since its cleavage product amyloid-$\beta$ acts as an
antimicrobial peptide~\todo{cite Soscia et al.\ 2010; Kumar et al.\ 2016}.

The second theme is lipid metabolism: the lipid-handling enzymes LCAT and
PLA2G15 (33 parasites) and the sphingomyelin synthases (32). Lipid uptake
narrowly misses the cut and leans extracellular: the BPI/LBP/CETP lipid-transfer
proteins (25 of 26 extracellular and 7 of 17 intracellular parasites),
apolipoprotein B (24 and 7) and the cholesterol transporters NPC1 and NPC1L1 (18
and 8). Many parasites cannot make all
the lipids they need. Tapeworms and schistosomes have lost the pathways for de
novo synthesis of fatty acids and cholesterol and take them from the
host~\todo{cite Berriman et al.\ 2009; Tsai et al.\ 2013}, and intracellular
protozoa such as \textit{T.~gondii} and \textit{Plasmodium} scavenge host
cholesterol and fatty acids~\todo{cite Coppens et al.\ 2000}. The convergence
on host lipid transport fits this shared dependence.

Other groups are helminth-specific and so outside the shared set: the netrin
receptors DCC/neogenin and UNC5, the sortilins, SPARC and CHID1 are reached by
24 to 26 helminths and at most three protozoa (Supplementary Table~S2).
Helminths are animals and, unlike protozoa, carry metazoan signalling families
such as the netrins, whose receptors UNC-40/DCC and UNC-5 were first described
in \textit{Caenorhabditis elegans}~\todo{cite}. Shared ancestry with the host
gives helminth proteins the opportunity to act on host receptors directly, as
the TGF-$\beta$ homologue TGH-2 of \textit{Brugia malayi} does through the
mammalian TGF-$\beta$ receptor~\todo{cite Gomez-Escobar et al.\ 2000}. Netrin
signalling is not only neuronal: netrin-1 also restrains leukocyte migration
and retains macrophages in inflamed tissue~\todo{cite Ly et al.\ 2005; van Gils
et al.\ 2012}, so a parasite netrin-like protein could in principle modulate
the immune response around the worm. \todo{How many host orthologous groups
are reached in total?}

What each niche reaches on its own differs from what the two share
(Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:shared_ogs_niche}). There we rank groups within
each niche by the genera that reach them, as species of one genus are not
independent, leaving out each group's largest parasite group so that one
conserved parasite family cannot place a group alone. The extracellular ranking
is led by the integrin $\beta$ subunits (21 of 21 genera), the amyloid precursor
proteins (20) and apolipoprotein B (19). The intracellular ranking is led by the
histone-binding proteins RBBP4 and RBBP7 (7 of 8 genera), and 8 of its 15 groups
belong to membrane fusion, among them the VAMP and SNAP25-family SNAREs, the
syntaxins and the HOPS subunits. With only eight intracellular genera this
ranking is coarse: 12 of the 15 groups sit exactly at the cut-off.

Convergence within a genus, below what Figure~\ref{fig:shared_ogs} shows, is
rare. Of the 909 groups, few are reached by every species of one genus and by
no other parasite, and six of the nine genera represented by several species
reach none at all (Supplementary Table~S3). Almost everything a parasite
reaches is therefore also reached by parasites far from it. The exceptions are
the genera with the largest and best conserved networks: 78 groups for
\textit{Plasmodium}, 44 for \textit{Trichinella} and 8 for \textit{Leishmania}.
Only the \textit{Plasmodium} set is reached from many parasite proteins, 55
orthologous groups, rather than from one or two. A third of its 155 human
proteins belong to the actin cytoskeleton and the endocytic machinery, its two
most enriched processes against the intracellular host pool (endocytosis,
$\mathrm{FDR}=5\times10^{-9}$; actin filament organisation,
$3\times10^{-7}$), among them the $\beta$-spectrins, the capping protein
subunits CAPZA1, CAPZA2 and CAPZB and the class~I myosins. A blood-stage
parasite has to remodel the cell it lives in, and the knob-associated
histidine-rich protein KAHRP of \textit{P.~falciparum} binds erythrocyte
spectrin directly~\todo{cite Oh et al.\ 2000; Rug et al.\ 2006}; one of the
parasite groups reaching spectrin holds a knob protein homologue. The
\textit{Leishmania} set rests on two parasite proteins alone, a synaptobrevin
reaching the host SNAREs and the NADPH-oxidase subunits NCF1, NCF4 and NOXO1,
and an ATG8 reaching the host autophagy machinery, so it is the kind of
convergence the parasite-group count is there to flag.

  \caption{Human orthologous groups shared by intracellular and extracellular
  parasites. Rows are the human orthologous groups with a predicted interaction
  from at least half of the parasites of each niche (at least 9 of 17
  intracellular and 13 of 26 extracellular), ordered by the total number of

The host processes reached also split by niche rather than by taxonomy
(Figure~\ref{fig:parasite_go}). Each parasite is tested against the host
proteins it could have reached, those of its own niche that pass the filters,
so the split is not simply a consequence of the localization filter. Every
parasite except \textit{T.~hominis}, which has a single prediction, reaches at
least one over-represented process.

Among the 16 intracellular parasites, autophagy is shared: 15 are enriched for
autophagosome organisation and all 16 for autophagosome maturation. Autophagy
is a cell-autonomous defence against intracellular pathogens, and
intracellular parasites both evade and exploit it. The vacuole of
\textit{Plasmodium} liver stages is decorated with host LC3, which the
parasite tolerates and may use to acquire nutrients~\todo{cite Prado et al.\
2015; Real et al.\ 2018}; host autophagy promotes \textit{T.~cruzi}
invasion~\todo{cite Romano et al.\ 2009}; and \textit{T.~gondii} keeps its
vacuole out of reach of autophagic killing~\todo{cite}. The spliceosome (RNA
splicing, U2-type prespliceosome assembly and mRNA transport) is reached by
the five \textit{Trichinella} species, the three \textit{Plasmodium} species,
\textit{L.~braziliensis} and \textit{T.~cruzi}. For \textit{Trichinella} this
is biologically conceivable: the larva reprogrammes the infected muscle cell,
and its secreted products accumulate in the host nuclei~\todo{cite Despommier}.
For \textit{Plasmodium} in erythrocytes, which have no nucleus, it is not, and
we return to these links in the case study below.

The 26 extracellular parasites mostly reach the cell surface and its
signalling. All 26 are enriched for cell--substrate adhesion, 24 for
integrin-mediated signalling, 25 for lipid metabolism, and most for cell
motility and neuron development. Many of these worms penetrate and migrate
through host tissue: schistosome cercariae enter through the skin, hookworm
and \textit{Strongyloides} larvae travel through skin and lungs to the
intestine, and filarial worms settle in lymphatics or subcutaneous tissue.
Adhesion and integrin signalling are also how host immune cells are recruited
to and around the parasite. The enrichment for neuron development largely
comes from the axon-guidance receptors above, and so reflects shared metazoan
signalling families as much as neural tropism. A few processes are shared
across the niches, most clearly vesicle fusion and lysosomal transport (14
parasites of each niche). Intracellular parasites have to manage the host
endolysosomal system around their vacuole, and extracellular helminths release
extracellular vesicles that host cells take up~\todo{cite Buck et al.\ 2014},
so both kinds of parasite engage host membrane traffic, by different routes.

% paper/figures/parasite_go.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/parasite_go}
  \caption{Gene Ontology biological processes over-represented among the human
  proteins each parasite is predicted to interact with. Each parasite is tested
  on its own with a one-sided Fisher's exact test against the human proteins
  that passed the pipeline's filters, and corrected with Benjamini--Hochberg. A
  dot marks a process at FDR $\le 0.05$, sized by the number of the parasite's
  host interactors annotated to the process and shaded by the odds ratio. Rows
  are chosen per parasite: its processes are taken from the most significant
  down until two are represented, where a process counts as represented by a
  row already chosen if the two share at least half of their annotated human
  proteins, and is then not drawn separately. Hatching marks a process that
  cannot be enriched in that niche, because the pool it is tested against holds
  too few (at most 10) or too many (at least 500) proteins annotated to it.}
  \label{fig:parasite_go}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Comparing the hosts of one parasite}
Ten parasites were predicted against more than one host, and the hosts play
different roles in their life cycles. Rats are the definitive hosts of
\textit{Hymenolepis diminuta} and \textit{Angiostrongylus cantonensis}, and
wild rodents of \textit{A.~costaricensis}; humans are accidental hosts, in
which \textit{A.~cantonensis} larvae stray into the brain and cause eosinophilic
meningitis~\todo{cite}. Pigs are a main source of human trichinellosis. Mice
and rats are laboratory models: for \textit{Nippostrongylus brasiliensis},
\textit{Trichinella} and \textit{Leishmania braziliensis}, and, in the case of
the rodent malaria parasites \textit{Plasmodium berghei} and
\textit{P.~yoelii}, for the biology of \textit{P.~falciparum} itself. To
compare the hosts, we compare links between orthologous groups rather than
individual PPIs, since the host proteins differ
(Figure~\ref{fig:multi_host}).

Most of each interactome is shared between hosts
(Figure~\ref{fig:multi_host}A). This is expected, since the host proteins most
often reached are conserved across mammals, and it is consistent with the
ability of these parasites to complete, or at least begin, their development
in several mammals. Where the hosts differ, the host with fewer links is often
the natural one, such as rat for \textit{H.~diminuta} and pig for
\textit{Trichinella} (Figure~\ref{fig:multi_host}B), the opposite of what one
would expect if the differences reflected adaptation to that host.

\textit{P.~berghei} and \textit{P.~yoelii} are natural parasites of African
thicket rats and complete the same liver and blood stages in laboratory mice
and rats~\todo{cite}. Their interactomes are accordingly among the most
consistent between hosts, and most of what differs is lost from rat at the
expression filter. \todo{Expand the malaria comparison in mouse and rat.}

% paper/figures/multi_host.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/multi_host}
  \caption{Comparison of hosts for the parasites that infect more than one
  host. An interaction is compared between hosts as the pair of orthologous
  groups it was transferred from, so a link counts as shared when both hosts
  carry a protein of the host group interacting with the parasite's.
  \textbf{(A)} The predicted interactions of each parasite, coloured by the
  hosts in which they are predicted. \textbf{(B)} For each host, the links it
  lacks that another host of the same parasite carries, coloured by the first
  filter that removes it: absent from the host proteome, removed by the TISSUES
  filter, or removed by the DeepLoc filter.}
  \label{fig:multi_host}
\end{figure}

Three quarters of the links missing from a host are lost at the TISSUES filter,
and these losses follow how well each host's infected tissues are annotated
(Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:tissues_coverage}). Rat, for instance, has no
annotation for blood, skin or stomach, which costs it links of the parasites
living there, whereas \textit{A.~cantonensis}, which infects the well-annotated
lung and brain, loses few. Pig covers every tissue \textit{Trichinella} infects,
but with fewer proteins per tissue. Most of the differences between hosts thus
reflect differences in annotation rather than biology.

This is where having several hosts becomes useful, because one host can reveal
candidate interactions that the annotation of another hides. Human has no nose
or macrophage annotations, although the nasal mucosa is the site of
mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and macrophages are the cells the parasite lives
in~\todo{cite}, and it loses links of \textit{Leishmania braziliensis} at this
filter that mouse carries. Nearly all of these are reached in mouse through a protein
annotated in macrophages, and most of their human orthologues are detected in
macrophage clusters of the Human Protein Atlas, making them candidate human
interactions that the human network alone misses. ATG14, for example, is linked
to the parasite's ATG8C proteins in mouse and, among the infected tissues, is
annotated there only in macrophages, yet it is also expressed in human
macrophages. Mouse plays the same role for rat in the blood stage of the rodent
malaria parasites.

Comparing hosts also helps in choosing and interpreting a laboratory model.
Links shared by a model and a target host are those that the model could be
used to study, and they make up most of each interactome. Only a few links are
lost because the host has no member of the orthologous group, and these are the
candidates for genuine host differences: a host that lacks a parasite's target
cannot be reached through it. Their small number suggests that the conserved
core of these host--parasite interactions is largely the same across the mammals
studied. \todo{Name the host groups behind the pig and rat losses?}

\subsection{Case study: \textit{P.~falciparum}}
\textit{P.~falciparum} causes most malaria deaths. Its life cycle in humans
moves through several tissues: sporozoites injected into the skin travel to the
liver and develop inside hepatocytes, and the merozoites released from the
liver invade erythrocytes, where repeated cycles of replication cause the
disease. Infected erythrocytes adhere to the endothelium of the brain and other
organs, which underlies cerebral malaria, and are cleared in the
spleen~\todo{cite}. We used the cell-type resolution of OrthoHPI 2.0 to narrow
the predicted network to the blood stage (Figure~\ref{fig:pf_case_study}).

At a confidence score of at least 0.7, \textit{P.~falciparum} has 462
predicted links between 49 parasite and 278 human proteins
(Figure~\ref{fig:pf_case_study}A). Restricting to host proteins found in blood
keeps 274 links (B), and to those detected in erythrocytes 156 links between 35
parasite and 85 host proteins (C). Only three links, from merozoite surface
protein 7 (MSP7) and two MSP7-like proteins to the transcription factor NFE2,
involve a host protein found in blood but in none of the other tissues the
parasite infects (D).

The erythrocyte network is dominated by conserved eukaryotic machinery. The
largest modules connect parasite proteins to the host spliceosome (SF3B
complex, Sm and LSm proteins), and spliceosome terms are the most enriched at
every stage (Figure~\ref{fig:pf_case_study}E). Others connect parasite
proteins to clathrin and the AP-1 and AP-2 adaptors, to COPI, and to
phosphoinositide kinases. These links are unlikely to occur in the
erythrocyte: mature erythrocytes have no nucleus and have shed most of their
membrane-trafficking machinery, and the transcripts detected in the
erythrocyte cluster most likely come from reticulocytes and erythroid
precursors. Rather, the parasite proteins involved are members of the same
conserved complexes in the parasite itself. The AP-2 $\mu$ subunit, for
example, functions in the parasite's own endocytosis, and its variants are
associated with reduced susceptibility to artemisinin~\todo{cite Henriques et
al.\ 2014; Birnbaum et al.\ 2020}. Such links say more about the parasite's own
biology than about its contact with the host, and the cell-type view makes them
easy to recognise.

Other links point to host processes known to matter in infection, and are
better candidates for real contacts, although not necessarily in erythrocytes.
MSP3, a blood-stage vaccine candidate~\todo{cite}, and a parasite
WD-repeat protein are linked to the host autophagy proteins LC3, GABARAP,
ATG12, ATG3 and WIPI2. Host LC3 decorates the parasite vacuole in liver-stage
infection~\todo{cite Prado et al.\ 2015}, so these links are more relevant to
the hepatocyte than to the erythrocyte. Liver-specific protein 1 (LISP1), which
the parasite needs to break down its vacuole membrane at the end of liver-stage
development~\todo{cite Ishino et al.\ 2009}, is linked to the host ANP32
proteins, which influenza viruses hijack for replication and whose
species-specific differences restrict avian influenza in
mammals~\todo{cite Long et al.\ 2016}. Since the expression filter applies
only to the host, a link can pass a cell type in which the parasite protein is
never expressed; parasite stage-specific expression is needed to place each
link in the right part of the life cycle (Discussion).

The three blood-only links show how the filters narrow a network and where to
be careful. MSP7 and the MSP7-like proteins are merozoite surface proteins
involved in erythrocyte invasion~\todo{cite}, which makes the stage plausible,
but their partners NFE2 and NFE2L2 (NRF2) are transcription factors, so the
interaction cannot take place in a mature, anucleate erythrocyte. Both belong
to the host's response to oxidative and heme stress during the blood
stage~\todo{cite}, so the link is worth noting as a hypothesis about the
erythroid lineage rather than as a contact in the circulating cell.

% paper/figures/pf_case_study.png is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/pf_case_study}
  \caption{Case study: human--\textit{P.~falciparum} network, narrowed
  in stages: the predicted interactions with a confidence score of at least
  0.7 (A); those whose host protein is found in blood (B); and from these
  two branches, those whose host protein is detected in erythrocytes, at more
  than 1 normalized count per million (nCPM), in the blood single-cell RNA-seq
  data of the Human Protein Atlas (C) \todo{cite Digre and Lindskog 2023},
  and those whose host protein is found in none of the other tissues the
  parasite infects, namely skin, liver, brain and spleen (D).
  \textbf{(A--D)} The network of each stage, drawn as in the OrthoHPI app:
  parasite proteins as diamonds, host proteins as circles, and link width by
  confidence score. In (A) and (B), proteins and links that reach no later
  stage are greyed. In (D), a parasite protein is named by its STRING
  description, or by its gene name where it has none, and a host protein by its
  gene name; the links of (C) and (D) are listed in Supplementary Table S4. \textbf{(E)} Gene Ontology biological processes enriched
  among the host proteins of each stage (Fisher's exact test against the host
  proteins the pipeline could have predicted, Benjamini--Hochberg FDR $<$

  covering the same host proteins as a better one.}
  \label{fig:pf_case_study}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Structural modelling of interactions}
To test whether transferred interactions are structurally plausible, we
modelled 48 predicted interactions whose human counterparts are known to bind
directly, each alongside that human reference complex, using AlphaFold~3
(Figure~\ref{fig:alphafold_direct}). AlphaFold found a confident interface
(ipSAE $\ge 0.1$) for 20 of the 48 human references, but for only 8 of the
predicted parasite--human pairs (by ipTM $\ge 0.6$, 11 references and one
predicted pair). The reference usually scored higher than the predicted pair
(30 pairs higher, 6 lower, 12 tied), most clearly when it shared the predicted
human partner.

Two points follow. First, that more than half of the experimentally supported
human complexes were not modelled confidently shows that the test is
conservative: a low score does not rule out an interaction. Second, the weaker
scores of the parasite--human pairs are expected, since the parasite protein
has diverged from the human one the interaction was transferred from, and
binding interfaces can be lost with few substitutions. Links with a confident
model, such as Q4D3L1--DR1 of \textit{T.~cruzi}
(Figure~\ref{fig:web_interface}C), are the best candidates for experimental
follow-up.

% paper/figures/alphafold_direct.png is generated: `make figures`.

  confidence of predicted parasite--human links against that of the human
  interaction each was transferred from. The 48 links are predicted against
  human, eight from each confidence-score bin between 0.35 and 1, at most one
  per pair of orthologous groups. Each is paired with a human reference: a pair

  the links in each quadrant: an interface in both models, only in the

\end{figure}

\section{Discussion}
\todo{Complexes: STRING interactions can mean that they are part of the same
complex, not necessarily that those two proteins are in direct contact.}
\todo{Mention somewhere that we lowered the cut-off for TISSUES compared to the
previous version.}
\todo{Discuss false positives.}
\todo{Single residue mutations can change binding.}
\todo{The expression filter is only on the host side, so the parasites'
proteins are not filtered by life stage. We have very little transcriptomics
data for the parasites. Check what we have in VEuPathDB
(\url{https://veupathdb.org/veupathdb/app}). We can't include this at this
point.}
\todo{False negatives: parasite proteins that don't look like any proteins in
intra-species interactions.}

A single parasite protein can also generate a whole spurious module, and the
result can be convincing. The five \textit{Trichinella} species share 44 host
orthologous groups that no other parasite reaches, and 31 of them are
nucleolar ribosome-biogenesis factors, among them UTP4, UTP6, NOP14, NOC4L,
NOL6, BMS1, TSR1 and fibrillarin (rRNA processing enriched at
$\mathrm{FDR}=3\times10^{-30}$ against the intracellular host pool). The
pattern invites a nurse-cell reading, since the infected muscle cell
de-differentiates and its nucleoli enlarge~\todo{cite}. It is nevertheless an
artefact. Every one of these links comes from three parasite proteins: two are
the \textit{Trichinella} orthologues of TBL3 and IMP4, nucleolar
ribosome-biogenesis proteins themselves, which entered the secreted pool on
confidently predicted signal peptides (DeepLoc extracellular 0.97 and 0.94)
while being annotated only as uncharacterized; the third is a DNase~II
homologue that reaches all 31 groups at scores between 0.36 and 0.58. A
correct orthologous group and a confident signal peptide are therefore not
sufficient. When a conserved housekeeping protein of the parasite is called
secreted, group-level transfer hands it the host's copy of the module it
belongs to, and the enrichment that follows looks like biology.

\section*{Supplementary material}
\subsection*{Supplementary tables}
\textbf{Supplementary Table S1} (\texttt{funnel\_supplementary.csv}). One row
per host--parasite pair, ordered by host, then by niche and taxonomic group: the
host and parasite proteins surviving each stage of the pipeline, and the number
of predicted interactions of the pair. Supplied as a comma-separated file
rather than typeset, since the rows are meant to be sorted and filtered.

\textbf{Supplementary Table S2} (\texttt{shared\_ogs.csv}). The data for
the common host interactors plot (Figure~\ref{fig:shared_ogs}): every human
orthologous group reached by at least two parasites, with the helminths,
protozoa, intracellular and extracellular parasites that reach it.

\textbf{Supplementary Table S3} (\texttt{shared\_ogs\_genus.csv}). The host
orthologous groups reached by every species of one genus and by no other
parasite, for the genera represented by several species. One row per genus and
group: the group with the protein family it belongs to, the human proteins and
gene symbols reached, the number of parasite orthologous groups and proteins
the links were transferred from, and the range of confidence scores. The count
of parasite groups separates a convergence carried by many parasite proteins
from one driven by a single conserved protein.

\textbf{Supplementary Table S4} (\texttt{pf\_case\_study\_links.csv}). The
predicted interactions of stages C and D of Figure~\ref{fig:pf_case_study}, one
row per interaction: the stage, the \textit{P.~falciparum} protein with its
STRING identifier, gene name and description, the human protein with its STRING
identifier and gene name, and the confidence score.

\textbf{Supplementary Table S5} (\texttt{shared\_ogs\_niche.csv}). The data for
Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:shared_ogs_niche}: per niche, every human
orthologous group reached by at least two of its parasites, with the genera that
reach it with and without its largest parasite group.
